chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Safwan from al-'Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), regarding the saying of the Exalted: 'And to Allah is the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it.' He said, 'He must have what he will perform Hajj with.' I said, 'If Hajj is presented to him and he feels shy (due to poverty or lack of means)?' He said, 'He is among those who can do it, and why should he be shy? Even if it is on a humpless, tailless camel.' He said, 'If he is able to walk part of the way and ride part of the way, let him do so.'

As for what Sheikh (Al-Tusi) mentioned in the conditions of the one upon whom Hajj is obligatory, namely that he be free (not a slave), the view regarding this is that the obligation of Hajj applies only to one who has wealth. And since the slave does not own anything according to us, nor does he have control over his own self according to his choice, he is not among those addressed by the obligation of Hajj. This also indicates that the slave is not obligated to perform Hajj, as narrated...

key_terms.حِمَارٍ أَجْدَعَ أَبْتَرَ: A humpless, tailless camel (indicating modest means)
key_terms.شُرُوطُ مَنْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الْحَجِّ: Conditions for the one upon whom Hajj is obligatory

ai.seo_question: What constitutes 'ability' (istita'ah) for the obligation of Hajj in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the practical application of 'istita'ah' (ability), emphasizing that modesty or limited resources do not exempt one from the obligation as long as one can manage the journey, even by combining walking and riding. It further clarifies the juristic ruling that slaves are exempt because they lack independent ownership of wealth and self-control, a condition central to the applicability of the command. This reflects the Shia scholarly focus on the realistic capacity of the individual rather than absolute perfection of means.
